proposed_fields.title: US Agencies Pursue Separate Immigration Social-Media Screening Measures
proposed_fields.description_short: US agencies pursued separate social-media screening and data-collection measures affecting some visa applicants and immigrants.
proposed_fields.description_medium: TechPolicy.Press reported several distinct initiatives in spring 2025: visa revocations pursued by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, ICE collection of public online information, USCIS social-media screening for perceived antisemitism, and State Department vetting of some applicants with past Gaza presence. proposed_fields.description_long: TechPolicy.Press’s April 21, 2025 analysis describes separate immigration-related screening and data efforts rather than a single comprehensive surveillance system. It reports that Secretary of State Marco Rubio pursued visa revocations, that ICE used a contractor to collect publicly available material from online services, that USCIS announced social-media screening tied to perceived antisemitism, and that a State Department cable addressed visa applicants who had been in Gaza since January 1, 2007. These are distinct actions by different agencies and apply to different groups. The article does not establish continuous monitoring of all immigrants, the use of artificial intelligence to analyze everyone’s relationships or location data, or the full set of targeting and constitutional conclusions in the original account. The original title and long description therefore overstate the evidence by combining several reported measures into a unified system. A narrower account can describe the individual policies as reported, while treating broader claims about scope, technology, and effects as unverified unless directives or records substantiate them.

uncertainty: The single-comprehensive-system framing, continuous monitoring of all immigrants, universal AI analysis, and asserted constitutional or discriminatory conclusions are not established by the cited analysis.

proposed_fields.description_long: The American Association of People with Disabilities (AAPD) published a policy brief on October 29, 2024, describing Project 2025 proposals affecting Medicaid and disability services. AAPD says the plan would convert Medicaid toward block-grant or per-capita funding and limit home- and community-based services (HCBS), which many people with disabilities use to live independently. AAPD argues that these funding and eligibility changes could restrict supports and coverage; that is the organization’s assessment of proposed policy. The assigned sources do not establish that the Trump administration abolished ADA accommodations, eliminated ADA enforcement, implemented the Medicaid cuts described in the former long text, or forced disabled people into institutions. Nor do they establish a realized coverage-loss count. This entry is therefore narrowed to the documented advocacy warning about proposals and potential consequences, with attribution made explicit. It should not present projected harms as completed government action or describe all accommodations and community-living protections as already eliminated.

uncertainty: Claims that ADA enforcement/accommodations were abolished, Medicaid cuts were implemented, disabled people were forced into institutions, or coverage losses occurred are not established by the advocacy brief.

proposed_fields.title: Judge Blocks Trump Administration’s Federal Assistance Freeze in February 2025
proposed_fields.description_short: On February 3, 2025, U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan temporarily blocked the Trump administration’s federal assistance freeze.
proposed_fields.description_medium: NPR reported that a Washington, D.C., judge issued a temporary restraining order on February 3, 2025, blocking the administration’s federal assistance freeze. Reuters identified the judge as Loren AliKhan and reported that she extended a pause on the funding freeze while considering a longer order. These reports concern grants, loans and other assistance, not shutdown-related federal firings.
proposed_fields.description_long: On February 3, 2025, U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan of the District of Columbia issued a temporary restraining order in litigation over the Office of Management and Budget’s federal-assistance freeze. The court order says it granted the plaintiffs’ motion for a TRO and denied the administration’s motion to dismiss. NPR reports that the injunction blocked the administration from implementing, giving effect to, or reinstating the original OMB directives under another name, and said previously frozen open awards had to be released. The order arose after OMB’s January 27 memorandum directed agencies to review federal financial-assistance programs and temporarily pause covered activity. The court action was a temporary restraint during litigation; the cited sources do not describe a government shutdown or an injunction against firing federal employees. The original title and short description refer to shutdown-related firings, while the linked reporting and court order concern the separate funding-freeze dispute. This revised account identifies the court, date, instrument, and scope, and avoids describing the TRO as a final merits judgment.

proposed_fields.title: Trump Signed the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act on December 22, 2017
proposed_fields.description_short: The 2017 law lowered the corporate tax rate to 21% and included a temporary deduction for qualified business income.
proposed_fields.description_medium: Donald Trump signed Public Law 115-97, commonly called the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, on December 22, 2017. The statute changed individual and business tax rules; the Joint Committee on Taxation says it lowered the corporate rate from a graduated 15–35% structure to 21% and temporarily allowed a deduction for qualified business income. The entry avoids an unqualified claim about who benefited most.
proposed_fields.description_long: Donald Trump signed the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act on December 22, 2017; the enacted measure is Public Law 115-97. The law changed both individual and business tax rules. In its 2019 distributional analysis, the Joint Committee on Taxation describes the reduction of the corporate income-tax rate from a graduated structure ranging from 15 percent to 35 percent to a flat 21 percent. It also describes a temporary deduction for qualified business income. The JCT report compares the act’s distributional effects with the law in effect before enactment and provides separate analysis of business-tax provisions. These are concrete provisions that can be described from the statute and JCT analysis. The sources do not justify the prior short description’s broad characterization that benefits were “skewed” toward corporations and high-income earners without identifying a particular year, measure, and distributional table. This entry therefore states the signing date and selected statutory changes, while leaving broader distributional conclusions to a clearly specified analysis rather than treating them as self-evident.

uncertainty: The broad “skewed toward corporations and high-income earners” characterization lacks a specified year, metric or cited distributional result.

proposed_fields.title: Trump Directs End to FY2017–18 Aid Programs for Northern Triangle
proposed_fields.description_short: The State Department said it was carrying out Trump’s direction to end FY2017–18 aid programs for El Salvador, Guatemala and Honduras.
proposed_fields.description_medium: On March 30, 2019, Trump said the United States would end aid to El Salvador, Guatemala and Honduras amid migration disputes. The State Department said the next day that it was carrying out his direction to end foreign-assistance programs from fiscal years 2017 and 2018 for the three Northern Triangle countries. The reports establish an announced, specified cutoff, not that all U.S. assistance ended or every affected account was immediately terminated.
proposed_fields.description_long: On March 30, 2019, President Donald Trump said the United States would end aid to El Salvador, Guatemala and Honduras amid a dispute over migration. The following day, Reuters reported that the State Department said it was carrying out the President’s direction and ending fiscal-year 2017 and 2018 foreign-assistance programs for the Northern Triangle. The Associated Press likewise reported that the administration was taking steps to cut aid to the three countries. This supports a dated announcement and a defined set of assistance programs. It does not show that every form of U.S. assistance was ended, that all previously appropriated aid was immediately canceled, or that a permanent cutoff was implemented. The sources describe the administration’s stated migration rationale; they do not establish a separate political motive or quantify all disbursements affected. The original CNBC link is unavailable and the AP topic hub is not the relevant article, so the replacement citations are the contemporaneous Reuters and AP reports.

uncertainty: Do not characterize the action as ending all U.S. aid or as a permanent cutoff; reports identify FY2017 and FY2018 foreign-assistance programs.

proposed_fields.title: Trump Pardons Former Border Patrol Agent Gary Mark Brugman
proposed_fields.description_short: Trump pardoned Gary Mark Brugman, a former Border Patrol agent convicted of violating a detainee’s civil rights.
proposed_fields.description_medium: The Justice Department’s clemency list records that Trump pardoned Gary Mark Brugman on December 23, 2020. It identifies a Western District of Texas conviction under the offense label “deprivation of rights under color of law,” with 27 months in prison and two years of supervised release. The Fifth Circuit’s opinion says Brugman punched and kicked a non-resisting detainee after the group complied with orders. The sources confirm the pardon and case facts, but not a documented motive for clemency.
proposed_fields.description_long: The Justice Department’s official list of pardons granted by Donald Trump records a full pardon for Gary Mark Brugman on December 23, 2020. It identifies his case in the Western District of Texas, the offense as deprivation of rights under color of law, a sentence of 27 months’ imprisonment, and two years of supervised release. In United States v. Brugman, the Fifth Circuit affirmed his conviction under 18 U.S.C. § 242. The court’s account says that after a group of detainees complied with orders to sit on the ground, Brugman punched and kicked a man who was not resisting. The White House clemency statement emphasized Brugman’s military and Border Patrol service and listed supporters of his pardon request; that is the administration’s rationale, not a judicial finding about the underlying conduct. The available records establish the pardon, offense, sentence, and conduct described by the court. They do not establish a private motive for Trump’s decision or any connection between the pardon and a specific benefit.

uncertainty: No source establishes a private motive or quid pro quo for the pardon.

proposed_fields.title: AP Tracks Trump’s Campaign Promises and Assigns Outcome Labels
proposed_fields.description_short: AP's tracker follows selected Trump campaign promises and assigns statuses such as “Kept,” “In progress” and “It’s complicated.”
proposed_fields.description_medium: The Associated Press published an online tracker of selected promises Donald Trump made during his 2024 campaign. Its entries pair promises with status labels, including “Kept,” “In progress” and “It’s complicated,” and identify a reported method such as an executive order or diplomacy. The available snapshot documents the tracker’s format; it does not establish an effect on Trump’s messaging.
proposed_fields.description_long: The Associated Press published a project to track selected promises Donald Trump made during his 2024 campaign. The archived version reviewed here presents commitments alongside a status and, for some entries, a reported method of action. Its labels include “Kept,” “In progress,” and “It’s complicated”; examples of methods shown in the table include executive action, an agency announcement, diplomacy, or congressional action. The project therefore offers a promise-by-promise tracking format, rather than a single verdict on the administration. The live AP page currently exposes only its title in the focused text retrieval, so the archived copy is the source for the visible classifications described here. Because this is a changing tracker, those labels should be tied to the dated archived view rather than treated as current indefinitely. The available evidence does not establish a March 4 snapshot, totals across policy areas, or that AP’s labels changed Trump’s public messaging. This draft removes those unsupported comparisons and describes only the tracker and the classifications visible in the cited capture.

uncertainty: No evidence ties AP tracker labels to Trump’s public messaging, corruption or a comprehensive outcome count.
